# `( )` — Group / Scalar / Rows / Train

Parentheses round an expression group it. Without `⋄`, they hold one expression wherever they appear, including inside [brackets](brackets.qmd).

```apl
(2×3)+4            ⍝ 10
x←2 4 9
[(+/x) ≢x]         ⍝ 15 3
```

Parentheses round literal syntax make a scalar holding it: a literal, a strand, or glyphs separated by spaces. So `(+)` holds `+`, and `(+ -)` holds the vector `[+ -]`. Glyphs that touch form a train, so `(-×)` groups. Around a name, parentheses group whatever the name holds, so `(x)` is `x` and `(f)` is `f`. The text alone decides, so reading the code never depends on what a name holds. This gives a literal a spelling at every rank: `(1 2)` is rank 0, `[1 2]` is rank 1, and `[1 2 ⋄ 3 4]` is rank 2. [`⊂`](enclose.qmd) encloses any other array.

```apl
(5)≡⊂5             ⍝ 1
⍴(1 2)             ⍝ ⍬
x←1 2 ⋄ (x)≡x      ⍝ 1
≡(+)               ⍝ 1
≢↑(+ -)            ⍝ 2
f←- ⋄ (f)3         ⍝ ¯3
```

A line break inside parentheses counts as a space. So an expression can continue across lines. Outside brackets, spaces separate runs, and each run is evaluated first. So this means `(1+2)×(3+4)`:

```apl
total←(1+2
       × 3+4)
total              ⍝ 21
```

## Rows

With `⋄`, parentheses write a vector whose items are the rows. Each row reads as [brackets](brackets.qmd) do, so every row is a vector, even a row with one item. The rows can differ in length. A trailing `⋄` makes a one-item vector holding one row. A line break still counts as a space, so rows written over several lines need `⋄` at the end of each line.

```apl
(4 ⋄ 4 5 ⋄ 4 5 6)       ⍝ [[4] [4 5] [4 5 6]]
a←1 ⋄ b←2
(a b ⋄ b)               ⍝ [[1 2] [2]]
(1 2 ⋄)                 ⍝ [[1 2]]
```

Brackets with `⋄` stack their rows into one array instead: `[1 2 ⋄ 3 4]` is a matrix, and `(1 2 ⋄ 3 4)` is a vector of two vectors. A vector of strings or of names is written in brackets: `["ab" "cd"]` or `[a b]`.

## Trains

Two functions form an atop: `(f g)Y` is `f(g Y)`. Glyphs alone separated by spaces make a scalar instead, as above, so a train of bare glyphs is written without spaces.

```apl
(- +/)1 2 3        ⍝ ¯6
(-×)3              ⍝ ¯1
```

Three form a fork: `(f g h)Y` is `(f Y)g(h Y)`. Dyadic forks pass both arguments to each arm.

```apl
(+/÷≢)2 4 9        ⍝ 5
(+/ ÷ ≢)2 4 9      ⍝ 5
```

Longer trains group from the right. A fork's left arm can be a constant. The right arm evaluates first.
